1.explanation: The CSS for the overlay wrapper is imported in style.js (via main.scss) and defines the ‘.next-overlay-wrapper’ container without a width, so inline content collapses. The Overlay.render method actually outputs that wrapper div and applies any wrapperStyle prop. Popup.renderPortal is where wrapperStyle is passed into the Overlay without a default width. To fix the collapse bug you can either add `width: 100%` in the SCSS for .next-overlay-wrapper (style.js → main.scss) or inject a width into the wrapperStyle prop in Popup.renderPortal, both of which ensure the container spans the full available width for inline content.
1.bug_scenario: In the provided screenshot, an Overlay with inline content is collapsing to zero width because the wrapper/container div has no explicit width set. As a result there is no room for the browser to render the inline content and the panel collapses (you can see the wrapper positioned at top-left with only padding showing). Adding a width:100% to the overlay’s wrapper/container will allow inline content to take up the available horizontal space and prevent the collapse.

2.explanation: The Overlay.renderPortal method in overlay.jsx generates the wrapperStyle object (defaulting to an empty object) and passes it to the root <Overlay> wrapper. Because no width is ever set, in inline contexts the absolutely positioned wrapper has zero width and the content collapses. Adding `width: 100%`—either in the CSS for .next-overlay-wrapper (main.scss) or by augmenting wrapperStyle in renderPortal—ensures the popup wrapper spans its container and prevents collapse.
2.bug_scenario: When an Overlay is used inside an inline container (no block-level width constraint), its root wrapper collapses to zero width so its content cannot render properly. In the screenshot, the white popup is squeezed because its parent .next-overlay-wrapper is absolutely positioned without a width, so there’s no horizontal space for the browser to display the inline content.
